title: End of the Line? The Big Picture
summary: We have ridden from horses on wooden rails all the way to floating magnet trains. Railways changed where people live, what time our clocks say and how we go on holiday. Now it's your turn to imagine the trains of the future!

sections.heading: The Whole Journey in One Ride
paragraphs: Imagine a magic train that can travel through time as well as space. You climb aboard, the doors close, and the window becomes a screen showing 400 years of railway history rushing past. Let us take one last ride down the whole line before we reach the end of the track.

First stop: the 1500s, deep in a mine in central Europe, where miners push little carts along wooden planks, just as Georgius Agricola drew them in his book De re metallica in 1556. A few decades later, around 1603 to 1604, Huntingdon Beaumont lays the Wollaton Wagonway in Nottinghamshire, and soon horses are pulling coal wagons along wooden rails all over the coalfields around Newcastle. Wooden rails give way to iron, and in 1803 the Surrey Iron Railway opens as a public horse railway anyone can pay to use.

The window fills with steam. On 21 February 1804 Richard Trevithick's locomotive puffs along the Penydarren tramroad in South Wales, the first known steam locomotive to haul a load on rails, crawling at about 5 miles per hour. Salamanca, Puffing Billy and George Stephenson's Blücher follow in the coal mines. On 27 September 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway opens, the first public railway to use steam locomotives. Four years later, in October 1829, Robert and George Stephenson's Rocket wins the Rainhill Trials, and on 15 September 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens as the first true intercity railway, worked entirely by steam.

Now the train races across oceans and continents. Railway Mania grips Britain in the 1840s. In America, Peter Cooper's Tom Thumb loses its race with a horse in 1830, but steam soon wins the bigger contest. On 10 May 1869 the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah, joins the first transcontinental railroad, built in the west mostly by Chinese immigrant workers. Canada's last spike follows in 1885, and the Trans-Siberian Railway stretches about 9,289 km across Russia by 1916.

The scenery changes faster. Clocks across Britain switch to railway time; on 18 November 1883, the 'Day of Two Noons', North American railroads adopt standard time zones. George Westinghouse's air brakes and Eli Janney's couplers make trains safer. Underground, London's Metropolitan Railway opens in 1863, and electric tube trains follow in 1890. Diesel streamliners such as the Burlington Zephyr arrive in the 1930s, Mallard sets the steam speed record of 126 mph in 1938, and by the 1960s steam is fading from main lines.

Then, on 1 October 1964, a sleek blue-and-white Shinkansen glides out of Tokyo, and the age of high-speed rail begins. The TGV, ICE, Eurostar and China's vast network follow. Finally, the window shows a train with no wheels at all: Japan's SCMaglev floating through a mountain tunnel at 603 km/h on 21 April 2015. From about 5 mph in 1804 to over 600 km/h in 2015, a speed increase of roughly 75 times, in a little over 200 years. That is the end of the timeline. But it is not the end of the line.

sections.heading: Three Big Ideas That Never Changed
paragraphs: Locomotives went from wood-fired puffers to floating magnets. Carriages went from open wagons with no roofs to air-conditioned double-deckers with Wi-Fi. Yet under all those changes, three big ideas stayed almost exactly the same for about 400 years. They are the real secret of the railway.

The first idea is a smooth, guided track. A road lets a vehicle go anywhere, but that freedom costs a lot: the driver must steer every second, the surface must be wide, and the wheels sink into bumps and mud. A railway gives up that freedom. The vehicle can only go where the track leads. In return, the track can be made smooth and strong, the wheels are steered automatically by their coned treads and flanges, and many vehicles can be joined into one long train following exactly the same path. The miners pushing carts along planks in Agricola's woodcuts and the Shinkansen driver watching the signal screen in his cab are using the same basic idea.

The second idea is low friction. A hard steel wheel on a hard steel rail squashes only a tiny amount where the two touch, a contact patch about the size of a small coin. A rubber tyre on a road squashes much more, and that squashing wastes energy. As a result, the rolling resistance of a train wheel is several times lower than that of a car tyre. Maglev took this idea to its extreme by getting rid of rolling friction altogether.

The third idea follows from the first two: you can pull a huge weight with very little energy. On a good track, a single horse could pull many times more than it could on a muddy road, which is why the first wagonways were built at all. Today a single freight train can carry as much as hundreds of lorries. In 2001, in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, the mining company BHP ran one of the heaviest and longest trains ever recorded: 682 wagons of iron ore, about 7.35 km long and weighing nearly 100,000 tonnes, pulled by eight diesel-electric locomotives and driven by one person.

Even the width of the track remembers the past. The standard gauge of 4 ft 8½ in (1,435 mm) came from the colliery wagonways of north-east England that George Stephenson knew as a young engine-wright. The wagonways used about 4 ft 8 in; Stephenson used that width at Killingworth and on the Stockton and Darlington, then added an extra half inch on the Liverpool and Manchester to help wheels round curves, and other builders copied it. A popular story claims the gauge comes straight from the width of Roman chariots, but that is a myth: historians trace it to the wagonways, whose width in turn suited a horse walking between the rails. After Britain's Gauge Act of 1846 and the spread of British-built engines around the world, standard gauge became the most common gauge on Earth. Today more than half of the world's railway lines, roughly 55 to 60 percent, use it, including most high-speed lines. Other countries chose different widths, such as India's broad gauge of 1,676 mm, which is one reason a train cannot simply drive from one country's network onto another's.

sections.heading: How Railways Built the Modern World
paragraphs: Railways did not just move people faster. They changed how the whole world worked, and you can still see their fingerprints almost everywhere you look.

They shaped cities. Before railways, most people lived within walking distance of their work. Trains let cities spread out into suburbs, with workers commuting in each morning and home each evening, as we saw with London's Metropolitan Railway. Whole towns, such as Crewe and Swindon in England, grew up around railway workshops. In North America, towns were founded along new lines, and places the railway passed by often shrank. Grand stations like London's St Pancras, New York's Grand Central and Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus became the cathedrals of a new age.

They changed time itself. As we discovered in Part 13, before railways each town kept its own local Sun time. Railways needed one shared time to run safely and keep timetables, so they created railway time in Britain and standard time zones in North America in 1883. Governments followed later. Every time you check the time on a phone and it matches everyone else's, you are using an idea that trains made necessary.

They transformed trade and food. Coal, iron, grain, cattle, timber and factory goods could cross whole continents cheaply. Fresh milk, fish and fruit reached cities before they spoiled, and refrigerated wagons carried meat across America. Newspapers and letters travelled overnight. Prices for many goods fell, and farmers and factories could sell to far-away customers.

They invented holidays and day trips for ordinary people. Thomas Cook's first excursion on 5 July 1841 carried about 500 people from Leicester to Loughborough, and soon seaside resorts like Blackpool and Brighton were packed with families who arrived by train. Travel, once a luxury for the rich, became something working families could enjoy.

They created big business. A railway needed far more money than any one person had, so companies sold shares to thousands of investors, which helped shape modern stock markets. Running a railway also required timetables, accounts, standard parts, uniforms, rules and managers in charge of huge numbers of workers. Many ideas about how large organisations are run were first worked out by railway companies.

And they inspired other inventions. The electric telegraph grew up alongside the tracks, sending signals and time checks down the line. Railway engineering pushed forward iron and steel bridges, tunnelling, air brakes, electric motors and safety systems. Even painters, songwriters and storytellers were inspired, from J. M. W. Turner's painting Rain, Steam and Speed to countless train songs and the adventures of Thomas the Tank Engine.

sections.heading: Remembering the Costs Honestly
paragraphs: A good historian tells the whole story, not just the exciting parts. Railways brought enormous benefits, but they also came at a real cost, and many of the people who paid it were not the ones who grew rich.

Think first of the workers. In Britain, gangs of labourers called navvies dug the cuttings and tunnels by hand, with picks, shovels, gunpowder and wheelbarrows, often living in rough camps. On America's first transcontinental railroad, thousands of Chinese immigrants did most of the dangerous work for the Central Pacific, blasting tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada in deep snow, and they were paid less than white workers. Irish immigrants and former soldiers laid track for the Union Pacific. Similar stories were repeated in Canada, Russia, Africa and Asia. Many workers died from explosions, rockfalls, cold and disease. Because records were incomplete, nobody knows exactly how many, but it was certainly hundreds or more on some lines.

Think of the peoples whose lands the railways crossed. In North America, the railroads brought settlers, soldiers and hunters deep into the homelands of Native American nations. Treaties were broken, land was taken, and the vast bison herds that many Plains nations depended on were slaughtered until they almost disappeared. In India, the first railways were planned mainly to serve the interests of the British colonial rulers, carrying raw materials to ports and troops where they were needed, although Indians later made the railways part of their own national life.

Think of the accidents. Boilers exploded, bridges collapsed, and trains collided. The Tay Bridge disaster of 1879 and the Armagh crash of 1889 were terrible tragedies. But each disaster taught a hard lesson, and engineers and lawmakers responded with better bridges, continuous automatic brakes, interlocking signals, the block system and, today, computer train protection. The result is one of the great safety stories of modern times: per kilometre travelled, a passenger today is much safer on a train than in a car.

Think, too, of pollution. Steam locomotives filled cities and tunnels with smoke and soot, and burning coal released carbon dioxide that is still warming the planet. And when cars and lorries took over in the twentieth century, closures such as Britain's Beeching cuts left many towns without the railway they had relied on. Remembering all of this honestly does not mean railways were bad. It means that every great invention has winners and losers, and that the choices people make about how to build and use it really matter.

sections.heading: Railways Today: Bigger Than Ever
paragraphs: You might think trains belong in history books. In fact, railways today are busier than at almost any time in their history. The world has well over a million kilometres of railway lines, enough to wrap around the Earth more than 30 times. The United States has the largest network, more than 200,000 km, most of it carrying freight. China comes next, followed by Russia and India.

Some numbers are almost too big to imagine. In the year 2023 to 2024, Indian Railways carried about 6.9 billion passengers, close to one journey for every person on Earth, and moved about 1.6 billion tonnes of freight. It employs more than 1.2 million people, making it one of the largest employers in the world. In Tokyo, Shinjuku Station is listed by Guinness World Records as the busiest railway station on the planet; in 2018 an average of about 3.6 million people passed through it every day, using dozens of platforms and well over 200 exits.

Freight trains are giants too. In North America, ordinary freight trains often stretch more than a kilometre and a half, and some intermodal trains, carrying shipping containers stacked two high, are over 5 km long. In Australia's Pilbara region, iron ore trains about 2.8 km long carry ore from desert mines to the coast day and night. Because one crew and a few locomotives can move thousands of tonnes, trains are one of the cheapest and lowest-carbon ways to move heavy goods over land.

High-speed rail keeps growing. China alone has built more high-speed railway than the rest of the world put together, while Europe, Japan, South Korea, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia all run trains at 300 km/h or close to it. Many cities are building new metros and tram lines, and countries hoping to cut carbon emissions are electrifying old routes and encouraging people to take the train instead of short flights. Rail still carries only about 8 percent of the world's passenger and freight transport, so there is plenty of room to grow.

Even old ideas are coming back. Sleeper trains, where passengers go to bed in one city and wake up in another, had been disappearing across Europe as cheap flights spread. Then, from December 2016, the Austrian railway company ÖBB began building up its Nightjet network, and new night trains now link cities such as Vienna, Munich, Zurich, Hamburg, Rome and Venice. Many travellers choose them because a night on a train produces far less carbon dioxide than a flight and saves the cost of a hotel. In a way, it is a return to the great sleeping cars of George Pullman's day, only quieter, cleaner and powered by electricity.

sections.heading: Keepers of the Flame: Heritage Railways
paragraphs: Even though mainline steam ended in many countries by the 1960s, steam engines have not disappeared. All over the world, volunteers keep old railways running so that people can still hear the chuff of the blastpipe and smell the coal smoke.

The very first railway saved by volunteers was the Talyllyn Railway in Wales, a little narrow-gauge line only 2 ft 3 in (686 mm) wide, which runs about 11.7 km from Tywyn on the coast into the mountains. It opened to passengers in 1866 to carry slate and people. By 1950 it was worn out and about to close, so a group led by the author Tom Rolt formed a society, and in 1951 volunteers took it over. It became the first railway in the world preserved by volunteers. Two of its original locomotives, Talyllyn and Dolgoch, are still steaming, though many of their parts have been replaced over the years. One of the volunteers was the Reverend W. Awdry, who based the Skarloey Railway in his Railway Series books, the stories that gave us Thomas the Tank Engine, on the Talyllyn.

Today Britain alone has well over a hundred heritage railways, and there are many more around the world, from the Durango and Silverton in Colorado to steam lines in Germany, India and Australia. The Middleton Railway in Leeds, where Salamanca began work in 1812, still runs trains. Museums preserve the stars of our story: Puffing Billy and Rocket in Britain's national collections, Mallard in the National Railway Museum collection, and the 1804 Penydarren engine remembered in a working replica.

Some fans have gone even further and built brand-new steam locomotives. The A1 Steam Locomotive Trust spent from 1994 to 2008 and about 3 million pounds, raised largely from supporters, building Tornado, a new express engine based on an old design that had been entirely scrapped. It was the first new steam locomotive built for Britain's main line since 1960, and on 12 April 2017 it reached 100 mph on the East Coast Main Line. These volunteers prove that the railway is not just a machine. It is something people love.

sections.heading: A Railway Record Book
paragraphs: Before we reach the final platform, here is a record book to keep, gathering some of the most remarkable numbers from our whole journey. Each one stands for real people who planned, built, drove or rode the trains.

The oldest surviving railway bridge is the Tanfield Arch in County Durham, built in 1725 to 1727 for horse-drawn coal wagons, about a century before the first public steam railway. The oldest surviving steam locomotive is Puffing Billy, built at Wylam Colliery around 1813 to 1814 and now kept at the Science Museum in London. The first known regular fare-paying passenger railway service began on the Swansea and Mumbles Railway in 1807, with horses doing the pulling.

The longest railway line in the world is the Trans-Siberian, about 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok, covering a seven-hour difference in clock time; riding the whole way takes about a week. The longest railway tunnel is the Gotthard Base Tunnel under the Swiss Alps, about 57 km long, opened in 2016. The longest bridge of any kind is a railway viaduct: the Danyang to Kunshan Grand Bridge on China's Beijing to Shanghai high-speed line, about 164 km long, completed in 2010 and opened in 2011. And the highest railway in the world, the Qinghai to Tibet line, climbs to about 5,072 metres at the Tanggula Pass, so high that carriages carry extra oxygen for passengers.

For speed, the fastest steam locomotive is still Mallard, at 126 mph (203 km/h) on 3 July 1938. The fastest wheel-on-rail train is the French TGV that reached 574.8 km/h on 3 April 2007. The fastest train of any kind is Japan's L0 Series SCMaglev at 603 km/h on 21 April 2015. Just as impressive in a different way, the Shinkansen has carried billions of passengers since 1964 without a single passenger death from a derailment or collision in normal service.

For size and busyness, one of the heaviest trains ever run was BHP's 682-wagon iron ore train of 2001, nearly 100,000 tonnes. The busiest station is Shinjuku in Tokyo. The biggest high-speed network, by far, is China's. And the oldest railway still in use is hard to name exactly, because so many lines have been rebuilt, but the Middleton Railway in Leeds claims to be the oldest continuously working railway in the world, running since 1758 under a law passed by Parliament.

Records are fun, but notice what they really show. Almost every one was beaten by someone building on the work of others: Rocket on Puffing Billy, the Shinkansen on a century of electric trains, the TGV and SCMaglev on the Shinkansen. No great invention is the work of one genius alone.

sections.heading: Your Turn: The Railways of 2100
paragraphs: Now it is your turn to be the engineer. Remember how each great step in this story began: with someone looking at a problem and thinking, 'There must be a better way.' Huntingdon Beaumont wanted to move coal more cheaply. Trevithick wanted an engine strong enough to replace horses. The Stephensons wanted one reliable enough to run a railway. Westinghouse wanted to stop trains crashing. Hideo Shima wanted trains fast enough to change a whole country.

So what problems will the railways of 2100 need to solve? Here are a few to think about. How could trains run on 100 percent clean energy, even on remote lines with no wires? How could we build new lines without spending enormous sums, digging up homes or harming rivers, as the Chūō Shinkansen's long arguments showed? How could a train make a long journey feel as quick and comfortable as a short one, with room to sleep, work or play? How could freight move from ship to train to doorstep without a single lorry? How could trains stay safe in a world of stronger storms, floods and heatwaves that bend rails? And how could railways reach the places that still have none?

Try sketching your answer. You might design a solar-powered sleeper train, an automatic freight pod that drives itself the last mile, a station that is also a park, or something nobody has thought of yet. Write down how it works, what it would cost, who would use it and what could go wrong. Every real inventor in these 20 parts had to answer those same questions, and many of them got it wrong several times before they got it right.

The railway began with a simple wish: to make a heavy load easier to move. That wish turned wooden planks into iron rails, rails into a worldwide network, and a crawling 5 mph puffer into a floating train at 603 km/h. Somewhere, right now, the next great journey is waiting to be invented, and the person who invents it might be the one reading these words.

deepDive: Why has the railway lasted 400 years when so many technologies vanished? Physics is a big part of the answer. The rolling resistance coefficient of a steel wheel on a steel rail is typically about 0.001 to 0.002, meaning a force of only about 1 to 2 kilonewtons keeps a 100-tonne load rolling on level track; for a car tyre on asphalt the figure is roughly 0.01 or more, five to ten times higher. Trains also benefit from running in a line: each vehicle shelters in the slipstream of the one ahead, so a long train has far less air drag per tonne than the same goods spread across many lorries. Gentle gradients matter just as much; climbing a 1 percent slope adds a force equal to 1 percent of the train's weight, many times its rolling resistance, which is why railway builders spent fortunes on cuttings, embankments and tunnels. Historians debate how much railways actually mattered to economic growth. In a famous 1964 study, the economist Robert Fogel argued that if the United States had relied on canals and wagons instead, its national income in 1890 would have been only a few percent lower; he later shared a Nobel Prize in economics in part for such work. Other historians reply that railways' biggest effects, on standard time, large corporations, national markets, finance and the opening of the interior, cannot be captured by such a calculation. Similar arguments surround railways and empire: in India, scholars have shown that railways cut famine deaths by moving grain and lowering price differences between regions, while also serving colonial power and drawing wealth out of the country. Today's debates are about the future. Supporters of high-speed rail point to lower carbon emissions per passenger and the ability to replace short flights; critics point to enormous construction costs and say buses, better local services or electrifying existing lines may give more benefit per pound or dollar. Statistics also show why railways are trusted: in Europe, passenger rail has a fatality rate per passenger-kilometre many times lower than cars. The railway's long life suggests a lesson for inventors: technologies that rest on deep physical advantages, and that can keep absorbing new ideas such as steam, electricity, diesel, computers and magnets, can stay useful for centuries.
